analysis.one_liner: Expands the earned income and child tax credits for working families, paid for by raising taxes on corporations and the richest investors.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would roughly double the earned income tax credit, open it to workers as young as 18, and replace the child tax credit with a monthly payment of up to $350 per child, plus a $500 credit for other dependents. To pay for it, it would raise the corporate tax rate to 28%, quadruple the tax on stock buybacks, impose a higher minimum tax on very profitable companies, and stop letting households making over $1 million use lower capital-gains rates. It also requires the IRS to notify people who qualify for the earned income credit but did not claim it, and to pay workers the value of state earned income credits that are currently non-refundable.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income working families gain the most: a doubled earned income credit that now reaches workers as young as 18, monthly child payments of up to $350 per child that reach the poorest families in full because the credit is fully refundable, and a $500 credit for other dependents. Workers in states with non-refundable state earned income credits would get paid the value of those credits in cash, and people who qualify for the federal credit but never claim it would be notified. Higher-income households above the phase-out thresholds gain nothing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income working families with children

how_it_helps.text: Roughly doubles the earned income tax credit's match rate, raises the income amounts at which it starts phasing out, and extends eligibility to workers as young as 18 — a wage subsidy for low-income working households.

Replaces the child tax credit with a refundable monthly payment of up to $300 per child 6 and older and $350 per younger child, phased out for higher incomes, paid month by month rather than once a year at tax time.
Adds a $500 credit for other dependents, such as older children in college or adult dependents.
Ends the lower capital-gains rates for taxpayers with income over $1 million, so the wealthiest investors pay ordinary income rates on most gains.
Pays workers the value of state earned income credits that are currently non-refundable, and requires the IRS to notify people who appear eligible for the federal credit but did not claim it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations pay a higher income tax rate (28%), a 4% tax on stock buybacks, and a 25% minimum tax on profits above $5 billion. Investors with over $1 million in income lose the lower capital-gains rates and would pay ordinary income rates on gains. Some corporate tax costs can pass through to shareholders and, to a lesser extent, workers and consumers.

drawbacks.text: The corporate rate increase from 21% to 28% and the higher minimum tax on very large companies could reduce business investment, and economists debate how much of that cost eventually lands on workers through slower wage growth.

Paying the child credit monthly means families whose income rises during the year could receive advance payments they no longer qualify for and have to pay back at tax time, a problem that caused hardship during the 2021 advance payments; the bill's recapture rules limit but do not eliminate this risk [S3].

The bill requires new federal machinery — an online portal, presumptive-eligibility determinations, and monthly payments — that the IRS would have to build from scratch, and families with no recent tax filing could miss payments unless they affirmatively register [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted at working and middle-income families, and the bill pays for them by raising taxes on corporations and high earners, which is an honest way to fund them. Real drawbacks: the corporate rate increase and capital-gains treatment could reduce investment incentives and fall partly on workers and savers over time; the monthly-payment system with presumptive eligibility and recapture is complex to administer and could mean repayment demands for families whose income changes mid-year; and the $1 million capital-gains threshold is high enough that few wealthy households would actually pay ordinary rates on most gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has never taken it up, so it has gone nowhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Sykes introduced the bill on January 15, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax bills.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has occurred since; the bill's complete action history is the introduction and referral.
Only three House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, so it lacked the bipartisan backing that tax bills moving to a vote usually carry.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything — the bill sits in committee — but the industries and high earners who would have paid for the expansions are better off by default while it sits untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits untouched in committee

for.name: Rep. Emilia Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its expansion of the earned income and child tax credits.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — in the months since.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors are Democrats, and with Republicans holding a majority on Ways and Means and in the House, a tax bill raising corporate rates has no visible Republican support in the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill raises the corporate rate to 28%, quadruples the stock buyback excise tax, and imposes a 25% minimum tax on profits over $5 billion for the largest firms. For ordinary people this funds the family benefits; for the corporate sector it is a direct cost.

Households with income over $1 million would lose the lower capital-gains rates and pay ordinary income tax rates on gains. The top 0.1% capture a large share of capital gains today, so this is where the bill's costs concentrate.

Monthly child payments, IRS eligibility notices, and new state-credit payment programs would create new compliance and filing work, but also new revenue for firms in this sector. Effect is modest either way.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, only three Democratic cosponsors, and no committee action since January 2025, the bill is unlikely to advance this Congress. Most bills referred to Ways and Means without a hearing die at the end of the session; its provisions could resurface inside a broader Democratic tax package if one ever reaches the floor.
